the field is still far from having reached the required level of maturity.

a lot of work is still to be done before a reliable and convincing statement on the real sensitivity of the proposed detectors could be made, and the claim of a higher sensitivity for a particular scenario should not be taken for granted, unless the relevant aspects are carefully addressed and the relevant systematic errors have been quantified.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the lack of radio-purity of a detector is an issue which can be addressed only through the use of a radio-pure detector, or at least a very low background one, in order to perform a proper subtraction.
, in the end, the only way to claim higher sensitivity for a given experiment is to have a lower background.
, at the present time, the most promising approach to the direct detection of dark matter is the use of low temperature detectors, such as the ones based on superfluid helium-4.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in order to achieve a reliable sensitivity in the search for a WIMP signal, it is necessary to have an accurate knowledge of the detector background, which can be achieved through the measurement of a large number of background-only data sets.

, in order to reach the sensitivity required by the next-generation experiments, it is necessary to develop detectors which are intrinsically free of systematic effects, or to be able to identify them, and to develop techniques for their correction.

the use of Monte Carlo simulations at very low energies, as well as the application of multiple subtractors and handling procedures to the measured counting rates might lead to misleading results, and therefore to wrong conclusions on the detector's sensitivity.
